name: Algirdas
restingPlace: Cremated by pagan rite in a forest near Maišiagala
summary: Grand duke of Lithuania from 1345 to 1377, who doubled the duchy eastward into the Rus' lands, broke the Golden Horde's hold on Kiev at the Battle of Blue Waters, marched three times on Moscow, and ruled for thirty-two years alongside his brother Kęstutis without once fighting him.
title: Grand Duke of Lithuania

birth.note: A modern estimate rather than a recorded date. He was a son of Gediminas, and held Vitebsk as duke through his first marriage long before he held Vilnius.

death.circumstance: Died of natural causes after thirty-two years as grand duke, and was cremated with eighteen horses in a forest near Maišiagala according to the pagan rite.

quickFacts.knownFor: Expansion into the Rus' lands and the diarchy with Kęstutis

imageInfo.caption: Bronze equestrian monument to Algirdas in Vitebsk, the Rus' city he ruled as duke, sculpted by Sergey Bondarenko and unveiled in 2014. It is a modern imagining, not a likeness.
imageInfo.creator: Sculptor Sergey Bondarenko; photograph by Sikorka111
imageInfo.note: Licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 by the photographer. Algirdas held Vitebsk through his marriage to Maria of Vitebsk, which is the monument's justification; its erection was nonetheless contested, some Lithuanian commentators reading a Belarusian claim on a shared medieval past into it. The falcon, the armour and the face are the sculptor's invention — no contemporary depiction of Algirdas survives.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Algirdas took power in 1345 with his brother Kęstutis by deposing a third brother, and the two then ruled together for thirty-two years in an arrangement that has few parallels in medieval Europe. Algirdas held Vilnius and the east; Kęstutis held Trakai, Samogitia and the war against the Teutonic Order in the west. Neither tried to remove the other.

Facing east, Algirdas roughly doubled the duchy. Bryansk, Chernihiv, Novhorod-Siverskyi, Podolia and finally Kiev came under Lithuanian rule, most decisively after his victory over three Tatar princes at the Battle of Blue Waters in 1362. Three times — in 1368, 1370 and 1372 — he marched on Moscow and burned its suburbs without taking the new stone Kremlin, and he died in 1377 a pagan, cremated with eighteen horses, having named his son Jogaila to succeed him over his elder brothers.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Born about 1296 — an estimate, not a recorded year — Algirdas was one of the seven sons among whom Gediminas distributed the duchies of the realm. His portion was Vitebsk, which came to him by marriage to Maria, daughter of its last prince, and he governed there for two decades before he ever ruled at Vilnius.

Those decades mattered more than his eventual accession. Vitebsk was an Orthodox Rus' town with its own law, its own church and its own boyars, and Algirdas spent his formative years as a pagan Lithuanian prince governing Slavic Christians by consent. The policy he later applied from the Baltic to the Dnieper was one he had already practised in a single principality.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Algirdas is the best example in this archive of a ruler whose reputation depends on which enemy is describing him. The Rus' chronicles, written by churchmen in the towns he attacked, are the fullest source and they are grudgingly admiring: a prince of great cunning who told nobody his plans, abstained from wine and mead, and moved so fast that his armies arrived before news of them. The Teutonic chroniclers, who mostly faced Kęstutis, barely describe him at all — which is itself evidence for how the brothers divided the work.

The Orthodox tradition also holds the darkest charge against him. Three of his courtiers, Anthony, John and Eustathios, were executed at Vilnius in 1347 for refusing to abandon Christian practice, and are venerated as the Vilnius Martyrs; whether Algirdas ordered it under pressure from the pagan priesthood or permitted it to appease them, the killings happened in his city and under his authority. Against that sits a long record of Orthodox churches built and Orthodox law confirmed across his conquests, including by his own two Orthodox wives.

His own religion was argued over almost immediately. Hermann von Wartberge and later Jan Długosz insist he remained a pagan to the end, and the cremation with eighteen horses at Maišiagala supports them; some Rus' accounts claim a deathbed baptism and monastic vows, and a few modern Russian historians have read him as an Orthodox ruler throughout. The likeliest reading is the least satisfying one: a pagan who found it useful to be unreadable, in a realm where most of his subjects were Christians of one confession or another.

contentSections.title: The diarchy with Kęstutis
paragraphs: Gediminas had left Vilnius to Jaunutis in 1341, and by 1345 Algirdas and Kęstutis judged him incapable of holding it. Their coup was coordinated and bloodless: Kęstutis seized Vilnius in winter and handed it to his elder brother, and Jaunutis, after a failed appeal to Moscow, was compensated with the duchy of Zaslawye. Algirdas became grand duke; Kęstutis received hereditary right in Trakai and the standing of a co-ruler rather than a subject.

What followed is the genuinely unusual part of the reign. For thirty-two years the two governed a single state from two capitals, dividing it along the line of the threat: Algirdas faced east and south against the Rus' principalities, Moscow and the Horde, while Kęstutis faced west against the Teutonic Order and the crusading raids into Samogitia. Treaties with the Order were negotiated by Kęstutis, campaigns on the Dnieper led by Algirdas, and each acted for both.

The arrangement survived because it was a division of labour rather than a partition of sovereignty — there was one grand duke, and Kęstutis never claimed to be him while his brother lived. It is best measured by what did not happen: no civil war between them in three decades, in a dynasty that fought itself bitterly in the generation before and the generation after. Within five years of Algirdas's death his son and Kęstutis were at war, and Kęstutis was dead.

contentSections.title: Blue Waters and the Rus' lands
paragraphs: The eastern expansion was steady rather than spectacular for most of the reign: Bryansk, Chernihiv, Novhorod-Siverskyi and the Podolian steppe came in by conquest, marriage and the placing of Gediminid princes on local thrones, usually with the existing law and church left untouched. Algirdas married twice into Rus' ruling houses — Maria of Vitebsk and then Uliana of Tver — and the second marriage drew him into the long struggle between Tver and Moscow that shaped the rest of his career.

The decisive blow fell on the Horde. In the autumn of 1362 Algirdas met the armies of three Tatar princes of the western Horde — Khachibey, Kutlubuga and Dmitry — at the Battle of Blue Waters on the Syniukha, a tributary of the Southern Bug, and destroyed them. The date is not entirely secure: the Rogozhsky chronicler, the earliest witness, places the campaign in 1363, and a minority of historians have questioned how large the engagement really was.

The consequences are not in doubt. Kiev passed under Lithuanian rule and Algirdas installed his son Volodymyr there; Podolia was taken; the Horde's authority over the lands between the Dnieper and the Dniester collapsed, and its western frontier pulled back toward the Crimea. It was the first serious reversal the Horde suffered in the Rus' lands, eighteen years before Kulikovo, and it made Lithuania a Black Sea power.

contentSections.title: The three marches on Moscow
paragraphs: The Lithuanian–Muscovite war of 1368 to 1372 was fought over Tver, whose prince Mikhail was Algirdas's brother-in-law and was being steadily squeezed by Dmitry Ivanovich of Moscow. Algirdas answered the appeal and marched in November 1368, destroying a Muscovite covering force on the Trosna and reaching the city itself.

There he met the reason all three campaigns failed. Dmitry had replaced Moscow's oak walls with white stone in 1367, the year before, and the new fortifications held. Algirdas burned the posad and the surrounding country for three days and withdrew; he came again in 1370 with the same result, and a third time in 1372, when the two armies faced each other near Lyubutsk and made a truce instead of a battle.

The verdict on all three is mixed, and deliberately so: Algirdas never took Moscow and never intended to hold it, but he demonstrated that Lithuania could reach it at will, and the Treaty of Lyubutsk left Tver protected for the moment. The longer consequence went the other way. Moscow learned the value of stone walls and of the metropolitan's authority over the Orthodox of Lithuania, and the contest for the Rus' lands that Algirdas opened was one his successors gradually lost.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Algirdas died in May 1377, in his early eighties by the usual estimate, having ruled longer than any Lithuanian grand duke before him. His body was burned in a forest near Maišiagala with eighteen horses, his weapons and his ornaments, in the rite his father had received — the last such funeral of a Lithuanian ruler, as it turned out, since Christianity arrived within a decade.

The succession was his one destabilising act. He had many sons by two marriages, and passed over the elder ones to name Jogaila, the eldest son of Uliana of Tver, as grand duke. The choice was legitimate enough in a system with no fixed rule of primogeniture, and it was accepted at first by Kęstutis, who held to the compact with his brother even after his brother was dead.

It did not hold. Within four years Jogaila had made a secret treaty with the Teutonic Order behind his uncle's back, and within five Kęstutis was dead at Kreva and Jogaila's cousin Vytautas was in arms. The diarchy had depended on two men choosing not to destroy it; the generation that followed made the other choice.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: Algirdas made Lithuania into an empire of Rus'. By his death the grand duchy ran from the Baltic to the edge of the steppe and most of its people were Orthodox Slavs rather than pagan Balts, governed in Ruthenian by their own princes and their own law under the formula the chancery used for two centuries: the old is not destroyed and the new is not imposed. Kiev, the old capital of the Rus' lands, was ruled from Vilnius.

That achievement also set the terms of the duchy's central problem. A pagan dynasty ruling an Orthodox population, at war with a Catholic crusading order and in competition with Moscow for the loyalty of the Orthodox church, had to choose a confession eventually. Algirdas avoided choosing for thirty-two years. His son chose Rome in 1385, which won Poland and lost the long argument with Moscow over who spoke for the Rus' lands.

His reputation in the Rus' chronicles — silent, sober, quick, and arriving unannounced — outlived him better than any monument, since no image of him was made in his lifetime. The bronze rider at Vitebsk and the woodcut in Guagnini's chronicle are both inventions of much later centuries, produced by people who needed him to look like something.

keyAchievements.title: Victory at Blue Waters, 1362
keyAchievements.description: Destroyed the armies of three princes of the western Horde on the Syniukha, opening Kiev and Podolia to Lithuanian rule.

keyAchievements.title: Thirty-two years of diarchy
keyAchievements.description: Governed a single state from two capitals with Kęstutis, dividing east and west between them without civil war.

keyAchievements.title: Three campaigns against Moscow
keyAchievements.description: Reached the city in 1368, 1370 and 1372 in defence of Tver, burning its suburbs but never breaching the new stone Kremlin.

keyAchievements.title: The Rus' expansion
keyAchievements.description: Added Bryansk, Chernihiv, Novhorod-Siverskyi, Podolia and Kiev, mostly leaving local princes, law and church in place.

timeline.title: Becomes duke of Vitebsk
timeline.description: Marriage to Maria of Vitebsk gives him an Orthodox Rus' principality to govern two decades before he rules at Vilnius.

timeline.title: Takes the grand duchy with Kęstutis
timeline.description: The brothers depose Jaunutis; Kęstutis seizes Vilnius and hands it to Algirdas, taking Trakai and the west for himself.

timeline.title: The Vilnius martyrs executed
timeline.description: Three Christian courtiers are put to death in his capital, an act the Orthodox church has remembered against him ever since.

timeline.title: Wins the Battle of Blue Waters
timeline.description: Beats three Tatar princes on the Syniukha; the earliest chronicle dates the campaign to 1363.

timeline.title: Kiev enters the duchy
timeline.description: Installs his son Volodymyr at Kiev and annexes Podolia as the Horde's western authority collapses.

timeline.title: First march on Moscow
timeline.description: Destroys a Muscovite force on the Trosna and burns the suburbs, but the new white-stone walls hold.

timeline.title: Second march on Moscow
timeline.description: Returns in support of Tver and again fails to take the fortress, withdrawing after ravaging the countryside.

timeline.title: Truce of Lyubutsk
timeline.description: The third campaign ends with the armies facing each other and a treaty that leaves Tver protected for the time being.

timeline.title: Dies and is cremated
timeline.description: Burned with eighteen horses near Maišiagala, having named Jogaila to succeed him over his elder sons.

sectionImages.alt: Woodcut roundel of a bearded prince in plate armour with a plumed helmet, holding a mace.
sectionImages.caption: Algirdas in a woodcut from Alessandro Guagnini's Sarmatiae Europeae descriptio, printed at Kraków in 1578. The armoured prince with a mace is a Renaissance invention made two centuries after his death.
sectionImages.creator: Alessandro Guagnini
sectionImages.note: Public domain. One of a series of imagined portraits of the Lithuanian rulers in Guagnini's chronicle; the same series supplies the image used on this archive's article for his son Skirgaila. The plate armour and plumes are sixteenth-century dress, and nothing in the image derives from a source of Algirdas's own time.

succession.note: Shown for the senior grand-ducal title at Vilnius, which Algirdas held alone from 1345 to 1377. Throughout those years his brother Kęstutis ruled the western half of the state from Trakai as co-ruler, so this line of succession describes one office of a two-headed government, not the whole of it.

predecessor.note: His younger brother, left Vilnius by Gediminas in 1341 and deposed by Algirdas and Kęstutis in 1345; he lived on as duke of Zaslawye. No article in this archive.

successor.note: His son by Uliana of Tver, named over his elder brothers in 1377, who later took the Polish crown and converted Lithuania.
